sections.title: From high-level design to a timed answer

topics.title: The system design interview framework

kcs.statement: A system design interview answer moves through fixed steps in order: requirements, estimation, API, data model, high-level design, deep dive, then bottlenecks and trade-offs.
Drawing components before agreeing on requirements is the most common failure, because every later choice (store, cache, sharding) depends on the agreed scope and scale.

serves.reason: The 45-minute mock answer is structured by exactly these steps
Scoping a vague prompt starts from knowing which artefacts the framework expects

problem_ideas: Put eight shuffled interview steps (API, estimates, deep dive, requirements…) into the correct order
A candidate opens 'design Instagram' by drawing Kafka and Cassandra: name the step they skipped and what it costs them
Given a transcript excerpt, label which framework step each paragraph belongs to
Interviewer says 'assume 100M users' at minute 20: which earlier steps must be revisited?
Rewrite a rambling first two minutes of an answer into a framework-led opening
Decide which step to cut short when only 30 minutes are available instead of 45

depth_threads.title: How senior-level expectations shift time toward deep dives

lens.reason: Interviewers grade structure as much as content; this is the skeleton of every answer you give.

topics.title: Functional and non-functional requirements

kcs.statement: Functional requirements state what the system does for users (e.g. 'a user can shorten a URL'), each as a verb on an entity that later maps to an API endpoint.
Non-functional requirements state how well the system must behave (availability, latency target, consistency, durability, scale), and they drive architecture choices more than functional ones.
Asking for the read-to-write ratio early tells you whether the design is read-heavy (favour replicas and caches) or write-heavy (favour partitioned writes and queues).

serves.reason: The written list of functional and non-functional requirements is part of the observable product

problem_ideas: Sort 12 statements about a chat app into functional vs non-functional
Write five clarifying questions for 'design a URL shortener' and the default you'd assume for each
A URL shortener has 100:1 reads to writes; say which side of the design gets more attention
Convert 'it should be fast' into a measurable non-functional requirement with a p99 target
Spot the out-of-scope requirement in a list for 'design Twitter' and justify cutting it
Given a news feed prompt, decide whether eventual or strong consistency should be a stated requirement

depth_threads.title: Extended requirements: analytics, abuse prevention and how to park them

lens.reason: Requirements are the first five minutes of every interview and set up everything you justify later.

topics.title: Sketching the API for an interview prompt

kcs.statement: Each functional requirement maps to at least one endpoint with a method, path or RPC name, parameters and response, e.g. POST /urls {long_url} → {short_code}.
Any endpoint that returns a list (feed, messages, search) must be paginated, and cursor pagination stays correct when new items are inserted while offset pagination does not.
An interview API sketch names how callers are identified (API key or token) because it enables per-user rate limits and abuse controls later in the design.

serves.reason: A REST/RPC API sketch is part of the scoped-design product

requires.reason: Endpoints are derived one-for-one from functional requirements

problem_ideas: Write the three endpoints for a URL shortener (create, redirect, delete) with request and response shapes
A feed endpoint uses ?page=3; show how a new post makes the user see a duplicate, then fix it with a cursor
Choose REST or gRPC for a mobile client API vs an internal service-to-service call and justify each
Find the missing endpoint in an API sketch for a chat app given its functional requirements
Pick the HTTP status code for a redirect from a short URL (301 vs 302) and explain the analytics trade-off
Redesign a chatty API that needs 5 calls to render one screen

depth_threads.title: Versioning an API without breaking clients

lens.reason: Interviewers expect a crisp API sketch within the first 10 minutes; it anchors the data model and design.

topics.title: Data models from entities and access patterns

kcs.statement: An interview data model lists each entity with its key, main fields and approximate size per record, which feeds directly into the storage estimate.
The data model should be shaped by the access patterns the API needs (e.g. 'fetch the latest 20 messages of a chat'), not only by the entities' relationships.

serves.reason: A data model is part of the scoped-design product

requires.reason: Access patterns are read off the endpoints' queries

problem_ideas: List the entities, keys and field sizes for a URL shortener and total the bytes per record
Given the endpoint 'get latest 50 messages in a chat', choose the key that makes it one lookup
A Pastebin model stores paste text in the same row as metadata; argue for splitting it
Identify the access pattern that a proposed Twitter data model cannot serve efficiently
Estimate the size of a user record with name, email, bio and timestamps
Draw the relationship between users, follows and tweets and name the hottest query

depth_threads.title: Why store choice comes after, not before, the access patterns

lens.reason: A clear data model is how interviewers check that your API and storage choices fit together.

topics.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimation and powers of two

kcs.statement: A day has 86,400 seconds, rounded to 10^5 for estimates, so 1 million events per day is about 10 per second.
2^10 ≈ 10^3 (KB), 2^20 ≈ 10^6 (MB), 2^30 ≈ 10^9 (GB), 2^40 ≈ 10^12 (TB), so byte counts can be converted with powers of ten in your head.
Estimates round inputs to one significant figure and aim for the right order of magnitude, stating each assumption aloud so the interviewer can correct it.

serves.reason: Every capacity figure in the observable product is computed with these conversions

problem_ideas: Convert 500 million events per day to events per second in under 15 seconds
How many bytes is 3 × 2^30? Express it in GB
A candidate uses 86,400 exactly and spends 2 minutes on long division: show the rounded version
Estimate how many 1 KB records fit in 1 TB
Spot the order-of-magnitude error in a worked estimate that confuses MB and GB
Read 10 ms per disk seek from the latency table and estimate seeks per second for one disk

depth_threads.title: Why order-of-magnitude errors compound when you multiply estimates

lens.reason: Fast, stated-aloud arithmetic is what makes your capacity numbers credible in the interview.

topics.title: Estimating QPS and peak QPS

kcs.statement: Average QPS = daily active users × actions per user per day ÷ ~10^5 seconds.
Peak QPS is estimated as a multiple of average QPS (commonly 2–3×, higher for spiky events), and capacity is sized for peak, not average.
Read QPS and write QPS are estimated separately by applying the read-to-write ratio, because they scale with different components.

serves.reason: Peak QPS is the first figure in the observable product

requires.reason: Uses the 10^5 seconds-per-day conversion and rounding rules

problem_ideas: 200M DAU each post 2 tweets and read 100: compute write QPS and read QPS
A URL shortener gets 100M new URLs per month with 100:1 reads: compute redirect QPS
Ticket sale opens at 10:00 and 80% of a day's traffic arrives in one hour: estimate the peak multiple
Given average 5,000 QPS, size for peak using 3× and state the assumption
Explain why sizing servers for average QPS caused a Black Friday outage
Chat app: 50M DAU send 40 messages each; compute messages per second at peak

depth_threads.title: Diurnal patterns and global users flattening the peak

lens.reason: Almost every prompt asks 'how much traffic?'; peak QPS drives every scaling decision after it.

topics.title: Estimating storage per year

kcs.statement: Storage per year = new records per day × bytes per record × 365, plus media stored separately, multiplied by the replication factor if replicas are counted.
The retention period sets total storage: a 5-year retention needs about 5 times the yearly figure, so stating retention is part of the estimate.

serves.reason: Storage per year is part of the observable product

requires.reason: Needs powers of two and rounding to convert bytes to TB

problem_ideas: 100M new URLs per month at 500 bytes each: storage over 5 years
10% of 400M daily tweets carry a 200 KB photo: yearly media storage
Recompute a storage estimate when the interviewer adds 3× replication
Chat app storing 20B messages per day at 100 bytes: storage per year
Spot the missing ×365 in a worked storage estimate
Decide whether text metadata or media dominates storage for an Instagram-like app

depth_threads.title: Compression, tiering and deleting expired data

lens.reason: Storage figures justify your choice of store and sharding later, and interviewers check the arithmetic.

topics.title: Estimating ingress and egress bandwidth

kcs.statement: Bandwidth = QPS × payload size per request, computed separately for ingress (writes/uploads) and egress (reads/downloads).
In read-heavy media systems egress bandwidth dwarfs ingress, which is the number that justifies serving content from edge locations.

serves.reason: Bandwidth is part of the observable product

requires.reason: Bandwidth is computed from read and write QPS

problem_ideas: 40 writes/s of 500-byte URLs and 4,000 reads/s: ingress and egress in KB/s
Video service: 1M concurrent viewers at 5 Mbps: egress in Gbps
Convert 2 GB/s to Gbps and say whether one 10 Gbps NIC is enough
Photo app: 1,000 uploads/s at 2 MB: ingress per second and per day
A candidate multiplies bandwidth by storage size instead of request size: find the error
Compare egress for serving thumbnails vs originals in a feed

depth_threads.title: Bits vs bytes: the factor of 8 that breaks estimates

lens.reason: Bandwidth numbers are what make a CDN or object store a justified choice rather than a reflex.

topics.title: Estimating servers and hot-data memory

kcs.statement: Servers needed ≈ peak QPS ÷ sustainable QPS per server, rounded up with headroom (e.g. run at ≤ 70% utilisation).

Cache memory ≈ number of distinct hot objects × average cached-object size, plus metadata and replication overhead; the hot set is estimated from unique-object counts and popularity (e.g. the most-read 20% of distinct objects), because counting every read request double-counts repeated reads of the same object.

requires.reason: Server count starts from peak QPS

problem_ideas: Peak 60,000 QPS and 2,000 QPS per server at 70% target: how many servers?
URL shortener with 50M distinct URLs read per day at 500 bytes each: memory to cache the most-read 20% of them, plus 30% overhead
A worked estimate caches 0.2 × 350M daily redirects × 500 bytes: explain why it overcounts and recompute from distinct URLs
Use Little's law: 10,000 QPS at 200 ms latency means how many requests in flight?
Decide whether the hot set fits on one 64 GB machine or needs several
Recompute server count after the interviewer halves per-server throughput

depth_threads.title: Why utilisation near 100% blows up queueing latency
Zipf popularity and how hit rate grows with cache size

lens.reason: Useful polish that impresses interviewers, but not one of the three core capacity figures.

topics.title: Drawing the high-level design

kcs.statement: A high-level design traces each core request from client through the application tier to the data tier, with one box per responsibility and arrows labelled by API call.
Start the high-level design with the simplest version that meets the functional requirements, then add components only when an estimate or non-functional requirement demands them.

serves.reason: The high-level design is a required section of the full mock answer

requires.reason: Components are justified against functional and non-functional requirements

problem_ideas: Draw the minimal boxes for a Pastebin: client, app server, metadata store, blob store
Trace a 'create short URL' request and a 'redirect' request through the same diagram
Remove the unjustified component from a 12-box design for a 1,000-user app
Split the read path and write path of a news feed into separate arrows
Name the box that owns each functional requirement in a chat app diagram
Explain to an interviewer why you started with a single database

depth_threads.title: Separating read and write paths as a design move

lens.reason: The diagram is the centrepiece interviewers remember; a clean request path earns trust.

topics.title: Deep dives, bottlenecks and trade-offs

kcs.statement: A bottleneck is the component that saturates first as load grows; you find it by comparing peak qps, storage and bandwidth estimates against what one instance of each component can handle.
In the deep dive, pick the one or two components with the hardest requirement (highest load or strictest consistency) and detail them instead of spreading time evenly.
Every design choice is stated as a trade-off naming what is gained and what is given up (e.g. lower latency for staler data).

serves.reason: Deep dive and bottlenecks are required sections of the mock answer

requires.reason: Bottlenecks are located on the high-level design
Saturation is judged against peak QPS

problem_ideas: A single database handles 5,000 QPS but peak reads are 40,000: name the bottleneck and the next question to ask
Choose the deep-dive component for a URL shortener vs for a chat app and justify
Rewrite 'use NoSQL because it scales' as an explicit trade-off
Rank three components in a feed design by which saturates first
Interviewer asks 'what breaks at 10× traffic?': produce a structured answer
Spot the design whose bottleneck is bandwidth rather than QPS

depth_threads.title: Amdahl-style thinking: fixing the slowest stage first

lens.reason: The deep dive is where interviewers separate levels; naming bottlenecks from numbers is the signal.

topics.title: Budgeting 45 minutes: a first timed walkthrough

kcs.statement: A workable 45-minute budget is roughly 5 min requirements, 5 min estimates, 5 min API and data model, 10–15 min high-level design, 10–15 min deep dive and bottlenecks, with a few minutes for questions.
Announcing each transition ('requirements are set, now estimates') keeps the interviewer aligned and lets them redirect time before it is lost.

serves.reason: Running the full answer under time needs an explicit time budget

requires.reason: The budget allocates time across the framework's steps
The final block of time is the deep dive and bottlenecks

problem_ideas: A candidate reaches the diagram at minute 28: identify where time leaked and re-budget
Allocate a 35-minute variant of the budget and say which step shrinks
Write the one-sentence signposts for each transition in a URL shortener answer
Interviewer says 'skip estimates': redistribute the freed minutes
Run a 10-minute speed version of a Pastebin answer covering requirements to diagram
Judge two transcripts: which kept the interviewer in control of depth?

depth_threads.title: Reading interviewer hints to pick the deep-dive topic

lens.reason: Running out of time before the deep dive is the most common reason good candidates get marked down.
